title: Concussion: a blow to the head and recovery
description: A concussion is a mild brain injury from a blow or jolt to the head. The brain goes through an energy crisis and, for a time, works differently. The episode follows the first moments, the days after, and recovery over about a month, as seen in research on athletes and pooled studies of mild brain injury.
caveat: The first two phases, the chemical surge and the energy crisis, are known mainly from animal studies, and no brain region is drawn for them because the injury affects the brain broadly. The blood-flow findings come from one study of 44 college football players, 17 of whom were scanned three times, and the activity finding from a pooled analysis of seven small studies. In the blood-flow regions, the dimming shows lower blood flow, not measured activity. In this study, symptoms eased within a week to a month, and some athletes were slower to recover. Reduced blood flow was already found about a day after injury, earlier than the regions are drawn changing. Whether concussions can have lasting effects is an area of active research and is not shown here.

phases.name: The blow
phases.caption: The blow sets off a sudden flow of charged particles and a release of the chemical messenger glutamate. This affects the brain broadly, so no single region is drawn.

phases.name: Energy crisis
phases.caption: This creates heavy energy demands, and the injured brain goes through a period of metabolic crisis.

order.rationale: The sequence from chemical surge to energy crisis comes from animal models, summarised in a review.

phases.name: The first week
phases.caption: Blood flow is lower than usual in the right insula and nearby temporal cortex. During thinking tasks, the right middle frontal gyrus, involved in attention, is less active. Slower reactions usually ease within a week.

order.rationale: The blood-flow study scanned athletes about a day and a week after injury; placing those findings after the energy crisis follows the animal timeline.

phases.name: Recovery
phases.caption: Over about a month blood flow recovers, and mood and anxiety symptoms ease. In athletes who were slower to recover, blood flow in part of the insula was still low at one month.

citations.title: Recovery of cerebral blood flow following sports-related concussion.
citations.quote: Imaging data suggested both cross-sectional (ie, healthy vs concussed athletes; P < .05) and longitudinal (1 day and 1 week vs 1 month postinjury; P < .001) evidence of CBF recovery in the right insular and superior temporal cortex.

regions.explanation: Blood flow in the right insula was lower than in healthy athletes in the first week after concussion and recovered by about a month. In athletes who took longer to recover, blood flow in the middle of the insula was still low at one month. From one study of 44 players, 17 of them scanned three times. The dimming shows lower blood flow, not measured activity.

regions.explanation: During thinking tasks in the first days and weeks after a mild brain injury, the right middle frontal gyrus, involved in attention, was less active than in healthy people. This was the only consistent finding in a pooled analysis of seven small studies. Those studies did not follow people further, so its return to normal is drawn as an assumption.
